title: Sholeh Zard
subtitle: Persian saffron rice pudding
excerpt: Sholeh Zard is a fragrant Persian rice pudding coloured a deep gold with saffron and perfumed with rose water and cardamom. It is served chilled and decorated with cinnamon and pistachios. Serves 6.
sourceNotes: Sholeh Zard has been made in Iran for centuries and is one of the oldest Persian desserts. Its name means yellow flame, a reference to the saffron-gold colour.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 2 days ahead and keep refrigerated. The pudding thickens further as it chills.

glossaryTerms.definition: Literally 'yellow flame' in Persian, a fragrant saffron rice pudding eaten chilled and decorated with cinnamon and nuts.
Distilled water infused with rose petals, used widely in Persian, Turkish and South Asian sweets to give a delicate floral flavour.

content.text: Place the rinsed rice and water in the large saucepan. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat. Reduce heat to low, cover and cook for 30 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes. The rice should be very soft and the mixture should be thick and porridge-like.

Add the sugar, butter, saffron water and cardamom. Stir until the sugar and butter are fully dissolved. Continue cooking over low heat for a further 15 to 20 minutes, stirring frequently, until the pudding reaches the consistency of thick porridge.
Remove from the heat. Stir in the rose water. Do not add the rose water during cooking as the heat drives off the floral aroma.
Pour the pudding into a large shallow serving dish or individual bowls. Smooth the surface.
Decorate the surface with patterns of ground cinnamon, flaked almonds and chopped pistachios. Cover loosely and refrigerate for at least 1 hour until fully set and cold. Serve chilled.

attrs.problem: Pudding is too runny after chilling
attrs.solution: Cook for longer in the pan before pouring. The pudding should be very thick when warm, thicker than you expect, as it loosens slightly when poured and then thickens again on chilling.

attrs.problem: Pudding has stuck to the base of the pan
attrs.solution: Stir more frequently during the second stage of cooking. Short-grain rice releases a lot of starch and catches easily. Keep the heat at the lowest possible setting.
Steep the saffron in hot water for at least 10 minutes before using. Grind the saffron threads to a powder first with a pinch of sugar in a pestle and mortar to extract maximum colour.

content.text: Sholeh Zard is a ceremonial dessert in Iran. It is made for religious occasions, offered to neighbours and distributed in the street during festivals. Each family decorates theirs differently with the cinnamon and nuts. The decoration can spell out words or form geometric patterns. It is one of the most visually distinctive desserts in the Persian tradition.
